@ bc5092a1 U1.3.1.1 | Primary and secondary data
**In a sentence**
  Primary data is what you measure yourself; secondary data is what someone else measured that you then use.
**Key terms**
  **Primary data**: data generated first-hand by the investigator.
  **Secondary data**: data generated by others and collated by the investigator.
  **Collate**: gather and organise data from several sources.
**Definitions**
  **Primary data**: data you generate yourself, first-hand — by experiment, measurement, fieldwork, surveys or observation.
  **Secondary data**: data generated by someone else that you collect and use — from journal articles, government databases, reports, textbooks, websites.
**In this research investigation**
  The Unit 1 investigation is mostly based on **secondary data** (you research a question about a material and sustainability).
  You may include small amounts of primary data (e.g. a simple test of a bioplastic's properties).
**Strengths and limitations**
  Primary: you control the method and know its limitations; but limited by time, equipment and sample size.
  Secondary: large data sets and expert methods you couldn't replicate; but you rely on someone else's methods and may not know all their assumptions, and it may be out of date or biased.
**Going deeper**
  The same data can be primary for one person and secondary for another: a CSIRO scientist's measurements are primary to them and secondary to you.
  Research investigations often combine both: secondary data to frame the question, a small primary experiment to test one part.
**Connections**
  Quality of evidence: secondary data must be judged for authority and bias.
  Characteristics of primary data (Unit 2 investigation).
**Practice questions**
  A student uses Bureau of Meteorology rainfall records and their own pH readings of rainwater. Classify each.
    Rainfall records: secondary. Their own pH readings: primary.
  Give one reason a research investigation might rely mainly on secondary data.
    The question involves large-scale or long-term processes (e.g. global plastic production) that can't be measured in a school lab.
**Flashcards**
  What is primary data? :: Data you collect first-hand, e.g. from your own experiment or observations.
  What is secondary data? :: Data collected by others that you use, e.g. from journal articles or databases.
  Give one advantage of secondary data. :: Large data sets and expert methods beyond what you could do yourself.
  Give one limitation of secondary data. :: You depend on others' methods and may not know their errors, assumptions or biases; it may be outdated.
  Data from a government water-quality database is {{secondary}} data.
  Is published data from a journal article primary or secondary for you? :: Secondary.

@ dd3ac8d6 U1.3.1.2 | Evidence, opinion and anecdote
**In a sentence**
  Evidence is systematically gathered and checkable; opinions and anecdotes aren't, and science deals only with ideas that can be tested.
**Key terms**
  **Evidence**: information from systematic observation or experiment that can be checked.
  **Opinion**: a personal belief or judgement.
  **Anecdote**: a personal story or single observation.
  **Falsifiable**: able to be shown false by an observation or experiment.
**Kinds of information**
  **Evidence**: information gathered systematically (by observation or experiment) that can be checked and repeated, and supports or refutes a claim.
  **Opinion**: a personal view or judgement, which may or may not be based on evidence.
  **Anecdote**: a personal story or single observation ("my friend's car got better mileage on E10"). Not reliable evidence — one case, not controlled, open to bias.
**Scientific vs non-scientific ideas**
  **Scientific ideas** are testable and falsifiable, based on evidence, and open to revision when new evidence appears.
  **Non-scientific ideas** can't be tested by observation or experiment (beliefs, values, aesthetic judgements), or are presented without evidence.
  Science can tell you what is (e.g. how much CO₂ a process releases); whether you *should* do something also involves values.
**Using this in your report**
  Base claims on evidence and cite it. Label opinions as opinions. Don't use anecdotes as support.
**Going deeper**
  Anecdotes can be useful starting points for a question ("my plants grew better with coffee grounds") but not as support for a conclusion.
  Expert opinion counts for more than a random opinion, but it still needs evidence behind it; in science, evidence outranks authority.
  Values questions ("should we ban plastic bags?") use scientific evidence but also involve non-scientific considerations.
**Connections**
  Quality of evidence: judging how strong evidence is.
  Decisions shaped by more than science (key science skills).
**Practice questions**
  Classify: "A study of 2000 households found a 30% drop in plastic waste after the bag ban." / "I think bans are annoying." / "My neighbour says she uses fewer bags now."
    Evidence / opinion / anecdote.
  Is "compostable plastics are better than recyclable ones" a scientific idea as stated?
    Not yet — it needs defining (better how? measured by what?) before it can be tested with evidence.
**Flashcards**
  What is an anecdote, and why is it weak evidence? :: A personal story or single observation. It is one uncontrolled case and may be biased or unrepresentative.
  What makes an idea scientific? :: It can be tested by observation or experiment and could be shown to be false (falsifiable).
  "Bioplastics are better for the planet" — evidence, opinion or anecdote? :: Opinion (unless supported by data such as a life-cycle assessment).
  How does evidence differ from opinion? :: Evidence is systematically gathered and checkable; opinion is a personal view that may not rest on evidence.
  What makes a claim falsifiable? :: An observation or experiment could show it to be false.

@ 7cd87ab1 U1.3.1.3 | Quality of evidence
**In a sentence**
  Good evidence is valid, comes from an authoritative source, and has its possible errors and biases understood.
**Key terms**
  **Validity**: whether data measures what it claims to, using a fair method.
  **Authority**: the expertise and credibility of a source.
  **Peer review**: evaluation of research by independent experts before publication.
  **Bias**: a systematic distortion of results or reporting in one direction.
  **Corroboration**: support for a claim from independent sources.
**Validity**
  Data is **valid** if it actually measures or answers what it claims to — fair method, controlled variables, relevant to the question.
**Authority and reliability of sources**
  Ask: Who wrote it? What are their qualifications? Is it peer reviewed? Who funded it? When was it published? Is it cited by others?
  Strong sources: peer-reviewed journals, government science agencies (CSIRO, EPA), universities, reputable scientific organisations.
  Weaker sources: blogs, social media, advertising, sites selling a product.
  Check claims against several independent sources (corroboration).
**Sources of error**
  **Random errors**: unpredictable variation that affects precision; reduced by repeats and averaging.
  **Systematic errors**: consistent bias in one direction (e.g. an uncalibrated instrument) that affects accuracy; not fixed by repeats.
  **Personal errors (mistakes)**: e.g. spilling a sample — not a true "error" in data analysis; the result should be discarded and repeated.
**Bias**
  Bias is anything that makes results lean systematically one way: funding by an interested company, selecting data that supports a conclusion (cherry-picking), small or unrepresentative samples, leading survey questions.
**Going deeper**
  A quick source check (the CRAAP test): Currency (how recent?), Relevance, Authority (who?), Accuracy (evidence given? peer reviewed?), Purpose (inform, sell, persuade?).
  Conflict of interest isn't proof of bias, but it means the evidence should be checked against independent sources.
  Publication bias: studies with exciting results are more likely to be published, so the published literature can overstate an effect.
**Connections**
  Evidence, opinion and anecdote.
  Accuracy, precision and validity (Unit 2 investigation).
  Critically evaluating scientific and media texts (key science skills).
**Practice questions**
  A plastics manufacturer's website says its new bag breaks down in three months. How should you treat this claim?
    With caution — the source has a commercial interest. Look for peer-reviewed or independent testing under stated conditions before relying on it.
  What is peer review and why does it increase trust in a source?
    Independent experts check the methods and conclusions before publication, so errors and unsupported claims are more likely to be caught.
  Give one way to reduce bias when selecting secondary data.
    Use several independent sources, including ones that disagree, and choose data by pre-set criteria rather than whether it supports your view.
**Flashcards**
  What does it mean for data to be valid? :: It measures what it is supposed to and answers the question, using a fair method with controlled variables.
  Name three things to check about a source's authority. :: Author's expertise; peer review; publisher or funder; date; whether others cite it.
  Difference between random and systematic error? :: Random errors vary unpredictably and affect precision; systematic errors shift results consistently one way and affect accuracy.
  Give an example of bias in secondary data. :: A study funded by a company that sells the product being tested; cherry-picked data; unrepresentative samples.
  Repeating measurements reduces {{random}} error but not {{systematic}} error.
  What does corroboration mean? :: Support for a claim from independent sources.
  What is publication bias? :: Studies with striking results are more likely to be published, skewing the literature.

@ f4d2f552 U1.3.1.4 | Analysing secondary data
**In a sentence**
  To use secondary data well, organise it consistently, look for patterns, and judge how much each source can be trusted before drawing conclusions.
**Key terms**
  **Trend**: a general direction in data (increasing, decreasing).
  **Outlier**: a value far from the rest of the data.
  **Percentage change**: (new − original) ÷ original × 100.
**Organising**
  Record each source's full reference as you go.
  Put data into tables with headings and units; convert to common units so data from different sources can be compared.
  Group information by sub-question or theme.
**Analysing**
  Present data as graphs (bar charts for categories, line graphs for trends over time).
  Look for patterns, trends and relationships, and calculate means, percentages or percentage change where useful.
  Compare data from different sources: do they agree?
**Evaluating**
  Is each source authoritative and up to date?
  Do methods or conditions differ between sources (so data isn't directly comparable)?
  Is the data complete, or are there gaps, contradictions or outliers?
  Could there be bias?
  How confident can you be in a conclusion drawn from this data?
**Going deeper**
  Watch for data that isn't comparable: different years, units, methods or definitions (e.g. "recycled" meaning collected vs actually reprocessed).
  Correlation isn't causation: two things rising together may share a third cause.
**Worked example**
  Suppose a council's plastic recycling rate rises from 9.4% one year to 13.1% four years later. Calculate the percentage change.
    (13.1 − 9.4) ÷ 9.4 × 100 = 39% increase
    Note: this is a relative change of 39%, while the rate itself rose by 3.7 percentage points.
**Connections**
  Processing data: ratios, percentages and means (key science skills).
  Presenting data (graphs and tables).
**Practice questions**
  What's the difference between a 5 percentage point increase and a 5% increase?
    Percentage points are an absolute difference between two percentages (10% → 15%); a 5% increase is relative (10% → 10.5%).
  Why might two reputable sources give different values for the same quantity?
    Different years, methods, definitions, sample areas or units.
**Flashcards**
  Why convert secondary data to common units? :: So data from different sources can be compared directly.
  What should you do when two reputable sources disagree? :: Compare their methods, dates and conditions; look for more sources; state the uncertainty in your conclusion.
  Name two questions to ask when evaluating secondary data. :: Is the source authoritative and current? Are the methods comparable? Is there bias? Is the data complete?
  What type of graph suits comparing values for categories (e.g. different plastics)? :: A bar chart.
  Percentage change from 9.4 to 13.1? :: About +39%

@ e606a9ce U1.3.1.5 | Logbooks for collated data
**In a sentence**
  A logbook is the dated record that shows your investigation is genuinely yours and how it developed.
**Key terms**
  **Logbook**: an ongoing, dated record of all investigation work.
  **Authenticate**: show that work is genuinely the student's own.
**What a logbook is for**
  A logbook is a dated, ongoing record of all your work on an investigation. It **authenticates** your work — shows it is your own and how it developed.
  VCAA requires a logbook for the investigations; teachers regularly sight and monitor it.
**What goes in it (for a research investigation)**
  Your research question and how it changed.
  Every source used, with full reference details, and notes of what you took from it.
  Data collated from sources (tables, copied values with where they came from).
  Your analysis, calculations, reflections, and decisions (and why you made them).
  Dates on every entry.
**Good practice**
  Write entries at the time, not afterwards. Don't remove pages or rewrite; cross out with a single line.
  Record failures and dead ends too — they show your process.
**Going deeper**
  A good logbook lets someone else follow your thinking: why you chose each source, what you rejected and why, and how your question changed.
  Digital logbooks are allowed in some schools, but must be dated and not overwritten; check your school's rules.
**Connections**
  Using a logbook for primary data (Unit 2 investigation).
  Referencing sources: record full references as you go.
**Practice questions**
  Why should sources you decided not to use be recorded in your logbook?
    It shows your process and reasoning, and helps authenticate the work as your own.
  What details should be recorded for each secondary source?
    Full reference (author, date, title, publisher/URL, date accessed), what information you used, and your judgement of its reliability.
**Flashcards**
  What is the purpose of a logbook? :: To keep a dated record of all investigation work, authenticating it as your own and showing how it developed.
  Name three things a logbook should contain for a research investigation. :: The research question, full references for every source, collated data, analysis, reflections and dated entries.
  Why should logbook entries be made at the time rather than later? :: They are more accurate and they authenticate the work as it happened.
  Who checks your logbook during a VCE investigation? :: Your teacher, who regularly sights and monitors it to authenticate your work.
  Should rejected sources be recorded in the logbook? :: Yes — with the reason they were rejected.

@ 8bcd3bb8 U1.3.2.1 | Green chemistry and the circular economy
**In a sentence**
  Sustainable chemistry means designing products and processes that meet today's needs without harming future generations — using green chemistry principles and keeping materials in a circular economy.
**Key terms**
  **Sustainable development**: meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs.
  **Green chemistry**: designing chemical products and processes to reduce or eliminate hazardous substances and waste.
  **Atom economy**: the percentage of the mass of reactants that ends up in the desired product.
  **Renewable feedstock**: a raw material that can be replenished (e.g. biomass).
  **Circular economy**: keeping materials in use and designing out waste.
**Sustainable development**
  Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
  Balances environmental, social and economic factors. The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (17 SDGs) set targets such as clean water, affordable clean energy and responsible consumption.
**Green chemistry**
  Designing chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances and waste. The 12 principles include:
    Prevent waste rather than treat it afterwards.
    **Atom economy**: design reactions so most of the reactant atoms end up in the desired product.
    Less hazardous syntheses and safer chemicals (less toxic).
    Safer solvents (e.g. water or no solvent).
    Design for **energy efficiency** (room temperature and pressure where possible).
    Use **renewable feedstocks** (biomass instead of fossil fuels).
    Reduce unnecessary steps (derivatives).
    Use **catalysts** rather than excess reagents.
    **Design for degradation**: products break down harmlessly after use.
    Real-time monitoring to prevent pollution.
    Inherently safer chemistry to prevent accidents.
**Linear vs circular economy**
  Linear: take → make → use → dispose.
  Circular: design out waste; keep products and materials in use (reuse, repair, remanufacture, recycle); regenerate natural systems.
**Going deeper**
  Atom economy = (molar mass of desired product ÷ total molar mass of reactants) × 100. Addition reactions have 100% atom economy; reactions that produce by-products have less.
  Green chemistry prefers preventing waste over cleaning it up: it's cheaper and safer to never make the hazardous substance.
  The three pillars of sustainability — environmental, social, economic — must all be considered; a process that's green but unaffordable won't be adopted.
**Worked example**
  Calculate the atom economy for making ethanol by fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.
    Mass of reactants: 180.0 g mol⁻¹
    Mass of desired product: 2 × 46.0 = 92.0 g
    Atom economy = 92.0 ÷ 180.0 × 100 = 51.1% (the CO₂ is a by-product)
**Connections**
  Metal recycling and the circular economy; plastics and recycling.
  Biomass as a source of chemicals (renewable feedstocks).
  Applying sustainability concepts (key science skills).
**Practice questions**
  Why does addition polymerisation have 100% atom economy?
    All the atoms of the monomers end up in the polymer; there is no by-product.
  Name two green chemistry principles a bioplastic factory might demonstrate, with an example of each.
    Renewable feedstocks (plant sugars instead of oil); design for degradation (compostable product); energy efficiency or catalysis (enzyme processes at low temperature).
  What are the three pillars of sustainability?
    Environmental, social and economic.
**Flashcards**
  Define sustainable development. :: Development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
  What is green chemistry? :: Designing chemical products and processes to reduce or eliminate hazardous substances and waste.
  What does "atom economy" mean? :: The proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product; high atom economy means less waste.
  Name four green chemistry principles. :: Prevent waste, atom economy, safer solvents, energy efficiency, renewable feedstocks, catalysis, design for degradation (any four).
  How does a circular economy differ from a linear one? :: A circular economy keeps materials in use through reuse, repair and recycling and designs out waste; a linear one ends in disposal.
  Formula for atom economy? :: (molar mass of desired product ÷ total molar mass of reactants) × 100
  Atom economy of addition polymerisation? :: 100%

@ 2fd5a40d U1.3.2.2 | Sustainability in your research
**In a sentence**
  In your research, choose the sustainability ideas that really matter for your material and show, with evidence, how it measures up against each.
**Key terms**
  **Life cycle assessment (LCA)**: an evaluation of environmental impacts across a product's whole life.
  **Trade-off**: a gain in one area that costs something in another.
**How to do it**
  Identify which sustainability concepts are most relevant to your material or process. Don't just list all 12 principles.
  For each, explain how it applies with evidence: e.g. "PLA uses a **renewable feedstock** (corn starch) instead of crude oil" or "the process has a higher **atom economy** because…".
  Consider the whole life cycle: raw materials, manufacture, transport, use, end of life (recycled, composted, landfilled).
  Weigh trade-offs: a material can be better on one principle and worse on another (e.g. bio-based but not recyclable in existing streams).
**Useful questions**
  Where do the raw materials come from — renewable or finite?
  How much energy, water and hazardous chemicals does manufacture use?
  What waste is produced? What happens at end of life?
  Does it move towards a circular economy?
  Which SDGs does it support or harm?
**Going deeper**
  A simple life-cycle frame: raw materials → manufacture → distribution → use → end of life. Ask what energy, water, emissions and waste occur at each step.
  Comparisons must use the same functional unit (e.g. impacts per 1000 shopping trips, not per bag, if bags differ in reuse).
**Connections**
  Green chemistry and the circular economy (the concepts applied here).
  Quality of evidence: LCA data from independent sources.
**Practice questions**
  Why should a comparison of paper and plastic bags be "per use" rather than "per bag"?
    Bags differ in how many times they're reused; comparing per use (a functional unit) makes the comparison fair.
  Give one trade-off in switching from PET to PLA bottles.
    PLA uses a renewable feedstock but can contaminate PET recycling streams and needs industrial composting facilities that may not be available.
**Flashcards**
  Why consider the whole life cycle of a material in a sustainability evaluation? :: A benefit at one stage (e.g. renewable source) can be outweighed by impacts at another (e.g. energy in manufacture or no end-of-life recycling).
  What makes a sustainability evaluation strong? :: Selecting relevant concepts, applying each with evidence, and weighing trade-offs to reach a justified judgement.
  Give one sustainability question to ask about a new plastic. :: Is the feedstock renewable? How much energy does production use? Can it be recycled or composted?
  A new plastic is made from sugarcane but can't be recycled in existing systems. Which trade-off does this show? :: Renewable feedstock (a benefit) against poor end-of-life circularity (a drawback).
  What is a functional unit in a life cycle assessment? :: The common basis for comparison (e.g. per use, per 1000 trips).

@ 81782f45 U1.3.3.1 | Key terms and chemical conventions
**In a sentence**
  Clear science writing depends on precise terms and correct chemical conventions, so a reader knows exactly what you mean.
**Key terms**
  **Chemical convention**: an agreed way of writing chemistry — formulas, equations with states, IUPAC names, SI units.
  **IUPAC**: the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, which sets naming rules.
**Define key terms**
  Define the chemical terms central to your investigation early, accurately and in your own words (e.g. polymer, bioplastic, biodegradable, compostable, green chemistry, circular economy).
**Use chemical conventions correctly**
  Chemical formulas with correct subscripts and charges (H₂O, SO₄²⁻).
  Balanced equations with state symbols.
  IUPAC names for compounds; correct symbols for elements.
  SI units and standard abbreviations (g, mol, L, °C, kPa); correct significant figures.
  Structural formulas or diagrams where they help explain.
**Connections**
  Formulas and names of ionic and organic compounds.
  Chemical terminology and conventions (key science skills).
**Practice questions**
  Correct this sentence: "The sodium chloride solution (NaCl) was heated to 60 degrees and 0.5 moles was dissolved."
    "0.50 mol of sodium chloride, NaCl, was dissolved and the solution was heated to 60 °C."
  Why is "20 mL" better than "20 ml" or "20mls"?
    SI convention uses capital L for litre (to avoid confusion with 1) and a space between number and unit; units have no plural "s".
**Flashcards**
  Why define key terms at the start of a scientific report or poster? :: So the audience understands exactly what you mean and the chemistry is communicated accurately.
  Give three chemical conventions to use correctly in a report. :: Correct formulas and charges; balanced equations with states; IUPAC names; SI units and significant figures.
  Why use IUPAC names in a report? :: They are systematic and unambiguous, so every chemist knows exactly which compound is meant.
  Write sulfate with its correct charge. :: SO₄²⁻
  Why include state symbols in equations in a report? :: They show the physical state of each substance, which matters for what is observed and for the chemistry.

@ 71d30390 U1.3.3.2 | Effective science communication
**In a sentence**
  Good science communication is accurate, clear, relevant, concise and pitched to its audience.
**Key terms**
  **Audience**: who the communication is for (experts, students, public, policymakers).
  **Purpose**: what it's meant to do (inform, persuade, recommend).
**Qualities of good science communication**
  **Accuracy**: correct chemistry, correct data, no overclaiming.
  **Clarity** of explanations of concepts, ideas and models — define terms, use diagrams.
  **Contextual clarity**: explain why the findings matter and what they imply.
  **Conciseness and coherence**: every part is relevant; ideas are logically linked.
  **Appropriate for purpose and audience**: technical language for experts, plain language and analogies for the public; choose the right format (report, poster, infographic, talk).
**Going deeper**
  Pick one key message and support it: busy readers remember one idea, not five.
  Visuals do heavy lifting: a single well-labelled graph can replace a paragraph of numbers.
**Connections**
  Presenting findings and implications (Unit 2 investigation).
  Communicating for your audience (key science skills).
**Practice questions**
  Rewrite for a Year 7 audience: "Bioplastics exhibit reduced lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions relative to petroleum-derived polymers."
    "Plastics made from plants usually release less greenhouse gas over their whole life than plastics made from oil."
  Give two ways to make a scientific poster more effective.
    One clear key finding in large text; a graph or diagram instead of paragraphs; logical flow from question to conclusion; minimal jargon.
**Flashcards**
  Name the characteristics of effective science communication. :: Accuracy, clarity, contextual clarity (importance and implications), conciseness and coherence, and appropriateness for purpose and audience.
  How should communication change for a non-expert audience? :: Plainer language, defined terms, analogies and visuals, and focus on relevance to them.
  What does "coherence" mean in a report? :: Ideas are logically ordered and connected, so the argument flows.
  Give an example of overclaiming in science communication. :: Saying a material "solves plastic pollution" when evidence shows only a reduction in some conditions.
  What is the "purpose" of a piece of science communication? :: What it's meant to do — inform, persuade or recommend.

@ 1be87461 U1.3.3.3 | Models, theories and their limits
**In a sentence**
  Graphs, models and theories organise what we know, but each simplifies reality, so part of using one well is knowing where it stops working.
**Key terms**
  **Model**: a simplified representation used to explain or predict.
  **Theory**: a well-tested explanation of a wide range of observations.
  **Limitation**: something a model or representation doesn't show or explain.
**Representations of data**
  Tables, graphs, flow charts, diagrams — chosen to show patterns clearly. A graph can mislead if axes are truncated or scales chosen badly.
**Models**
  A model is a simplified representation that explains or predicts (e.g. the ball-and-stick model of a molecule, the "sea of electrons" metallic bonding model, a life-cycle diagram).
  All models have **limitations**: they leave things out. Example: ball-and-stick models don't show that electrons are spread out or the relative sizes of atoms; the ionic lattice model doesn't explain why some ionic solids dissolve and others don't.
**Theories**
  A well-supported explanation of a range of observations (e.g. VSEPR theory, kinetic molecular theory). Theories are revised when new evidence doesn't fit.
**In your investigation**
  Use a representation or model to explain your findings, and state at least one of its limitations.
**Going deeper**
  Every bonding model in Unit 1 has limits: the shell model can't explain subshells; ball-and-stick models misrepresent electron density; the ionic lattice model can't predict solubility; "sea of electrons" doesn't explain magnetism.
  Scientists use several models for the same thing and pick the one that fits the question — that's normal, not a weakness.
**Connections**
  Every structure and bonding topic in Area of Study 1.
  Using models and theories (key science skills).
**Practice questions**
  Give one limitation of the shell model of the atom.
    It can't explain subshell configurations or why 4s fills before 3d.
  Why might a scientist use a space-filling model instead of a ball-and-stick model?
    A space-filling model shows the relative sizes of atoms and the overall shape and surface of the molecule more realistically.
**Flashcards**
  What is a scientific model? :: A simplified representation used to explain or predict a phenomenon.
  Give a limitation of the ball-and-stick model of molecules. :: It doesn't show relative atom sizes, lone pairs or that electrons are spread out; bonds aren't sticks.
  Why do models have limitations? :: They simplify reality and leave out some features to make an idea understandable.
  How can a graph mislead? :: By truncated axes, uneven scales or cherry-picked data that exaggerate or hide trends.
  Limitation of the ionic lattice model? :: It can't predict which ionic compounds dissolve in water.

@ 0dbd21c9 U1.3.3.4 | Social, economic and political factors
**In a sentence**
  Whether a sustainable material is adopted depends as much on society, cost, law and politics as on the chemistry.
**Key terms**
  **Social factors**: attitudes, behaviour, health, community and cultural values.
  **Economic factors**: costs, prices, jobs and investment.
  **Legal factors**: laws, regulations, standards and bans.
  **Political factors**: government policy, priorities and international agreements.
**Beyond the science**
  Decisions about materials and sustainability aren't made on scientific evidence alone.
  **Social**: public attitudes, health, jobs, community impacts, cultural values.
  **Economic**: cost of production, price to consumers, investment needed, effects on industries and jobs.
  **Legal**: regulations and bans (single-use plastic bans, chemical safety rules, waste laws), liability.
  **Political**: government policy, subsidies, international agreements, election priorities.
**Example**
  Banning single-use plastic bags: environmental evidence of harm (science) + public support (social) + cost to retailers (economic) + state legislation (legal) + government policy commitments (political).
**Connections**
  Decisions shaped by more than science (key science skills).
  Green chemistry: the economic pillar of sustainability.
**Practice questions**
  Give a social and an economic factor affecting whether a café switches to compostable cups.
    Social: customer expectations and willingness to use a bin correctly. Economic: compostable cups cost more and need a commercial composting service.
  How can legal factors drive change in plastic use?
    Laws such as state bans on single-use plastics require businesses to switch, regardless of cost or habit.
**Flashcards**
  Give an example of an economic factor affecting adoption of bioplastics. :: They often cost more to produce than fossil-fuel plastics.
  Give an example of a legal factor in plastics use. :: State bans on single-use plastic bags or straws.
  Why aren't decisions about chemistry-related issues based on science alone? :: Social, economic, legal and political factors (values, cost, laws, policy) also shape them.
  Give an example of a political factor in a chemistry-related decision. :: Government subsidies or policy targets for renewable energy or recycling.

@ b54975eb U1.3.3.5 | Referencing and acknowledging sources
**In a sentence**
  Referencing credits others' work, lets readers check your evidence, and protects you from plagiarism.
**Key terms**
  **Citation**: a short reference in the text (e.g. author, year).
  **Reference list**: the full details of every source cited.
  **Plagiarism**: presenting someone else's work as your own.
**Why reference**
  Gives credit to others' work (avoids plagiarism), lets readers check your sources, and shows your evidence is authoritative.
**How**
  Use a consistent standard style (e.g. APA or Harvard): in-text citation (author, year) plus a full reference list.
  A full reference includes author(s), year, title, publisher or journal (volume, pages), and URL with date accessed for online sources.
  Acknowledge help from people (e.g. a teacher or technician) and images or data taken from others.
**Example (APA style)**
  Author, A. B., & Author, C. D. (2023). Title of the article. Journal Name, 12(3), 45–67. (The journal name and volume are in italics in a real reference.)
  In the text: (Author & Author, 2023)
**Connections**
  Logbooks: record references as you go.
  Referencing sources (key science skills).
**Practice questions**
  What is the difference between a citation and a reference?
    A citation is the short in-text pointer; a reference is the full entry in the reference list.
  Do you need to reference a diagram you redrew yourself from a textbook?
    Yes — the idea and content came from the source, so it must be acknowledged (e.g. "adapted from…").
**Flashcards**
  Why must sources be referenced? :: To credit others' work, avoid plagiarism and let readers check the evidence.
  What goes in a full reference for a web page? :: Author or organisation, year, title, website name, URL and date accessed.
  What is an in-text citation? :: A short reference in the body of the text (e.g. author and year) that points to the full reference list.
  What is plagiarism? :: Presenting someone else's words, ideas or data as your own without acknowledgement.
